title: Genesis 5. The Cup Passed Down.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 5. The Cup Passed Down.
This is the book of the generations of Adam.
When God created man, He made him in His own likeness.
Male and female.
He blessed them.
He named them Adam.
That was chapter one.
That was the Cup full.
Now the Cup passes down.
Adam lives a hundred and thirty years and fathers a son in his own likeness,
after his own image.
He names him Seth.
The image that was given in chapter one is now inherited.
But the vessel that carries it is different.
Adam was made from dust and filled with breath.
Seth is born from a man who is already dying.
The image passes through mortality.
Adam lives eight hundred more years.
He has other sons and daughters.
All his days are nine hundred and thirty years.
And he died.
Seth lives a hundred and five years and fathers Enosh.
He lives eight hundred and seven more years.
All his days are nine hundred and twelve years.
And he died.
Enosh.
Kenan.
Mahalalel.
Jared.
Each one lives.
Each one fathers a son.
Each one has other sons and daughters.
Each one's years are counted.
And he died.
And he died.
And he died.
The drumbeat that began in chapter three, dust you are,
and to dust you shall return,
plays out as a list of names.
The Cup passes from father to son.
And every time it passes, the one who held it dies.
The inheritance is life.
The inheritance is also death.
What was given in the beginning, breath, image, blessing,
moves forward through vessels that crack at the end.
Except once.
Enoch lives sixty-five years and fathers Methuselah.
After Methuselah's birth, Enoch walks with God for three hundred years.
He has other sons and daughters.
All his days are three hundred and sixty-five years.
And then, the pattern breaks.
Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him.
No "and he died.
No dust.
The Cup that passes through death does not crack this time.
It is simply taken.
The man who walked with God walked past death without passing through it.
What this means is not explained.
The text does not say why Enoch was taken.
It does not say where he went.
It says only: he walked with God, and he was not.
The thread that carries the image through mortality has one moment where mortality does not hold.
One crack in the drumbeat.
Then the rhythm resumes.
Methuselah lives a hundred and eighty-seven years and fathers Lamech.
He lives seven hundred and eighty-two more years.
All his days are nine hundred and sixty-nine years,
longer than any man named in the list.
And he died.
The man whose father was taken lives the longest life recorded.
And dies.
Lamech lives a hundred and eighty-two years and fathers a son.
He names him Noah and says:
This one will comfort us in our work and in the toil of our hands,
caused by the ground which the Lord has cursed.
The name is a hope.
The ground that was cursed in chapter three,
that swallowed Abel's blood in chapter four,
that has received every father in this list,
Lamech names his son against it.
Noah.
Comfort.
Rest.
The name of the man who will survive what is coming.
Lamech lives five hundred and ninety-five more years.
All his days are seven hundred and seventy seven years.
And he died.
Noah is five hundred years old.
He fathers Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
The Cup passes down.
Ten names.
One taken.
Nine dead.
The line that began with breath in a garden moves through centuries of death toward a man with three sons and a name that means rest.
The world that was filled in chapter one and drained in chapter three has not yet been judged.
But the man who will carry the Cup through what is coming has been born.
